sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Hwanin** (*hananim*) ​— Supreme ‌God, Heaven ‌· Lord ​of Heaven ​— belongs ​to the ​Korean tradition, ​where it ‌is catalogued ​under the ​domain "Supreme God, ‌Heaven". The ​name means ‌"Lord of ​Heaven"[^1].

**Hwanin** ‌is the ​supreme celestial ​figure who ​rules from ​heaven in ​the Dangun ‌founding myth in ​Korean tradition. ‌The name ​means "Lord ‌of Heaven" ​and belongs ‌to the ​domain "Supreme ‌God, Heaven." ​In the ​Samguk Yusa, ‌Hwanin is the ‌ruler of ‌heaven who ​answers the ​Buddha's request ‌for a ​land fit ​for his ‌teachings by ​sending his ​son Hwanung ‌to earth. Hwanin ​is not ‌a creator ​in the ​biblical sense; ​he is ​the apex ‌of a ‌celestial hierarchy ​that authorises ‌the descent ​of culture and ​law to ‌the Korean ‌peninsula.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌restores the ‌name as ​**Hwanin** and ‌serves its ​temple at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/hananim/). ​The restoration ‌needs no distinctive ​letters or ​diacritics its ​ASCII form ‌would lose, ​which places ​the name ​in Tier ‌2. The ​plain ASCII ‌form *hananim* ​survives as a ‌modern convenience ​imposed by ‌the early ‌domain-name system; ​the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the form ‌the project ‌defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Hangul ​as ​**하나님**. ​Etymologically it ​means ​"Lord of ‌Heaven"[^1].

​The ASCII ​form ‌*hananim* survives ​only ‌because ​the early ‌domain-name ​system could ​not ​carry diacritics; ​it ​is a ‌technological ​compromise, ‌not an ​ancient ‌spelling. The ​Unicode ‌restoration **Hwanin** ​recovers ‌the full ​diacritic ​detail ‌of the ‌scholarly ‌transliteration directly ​in ​the address ‌bar. ​The restoration ​needs ‌no ​distinctive letters ​or ‌diacritics its ​ASCII ‌form would ​lose, ​which ​places the ​name ‌in Tier ‌2.

​The letter-by-letter ‌transformation ​runs:

- ​**h** ‌→ ‌**H** — ‌Same, ‌capitalized
- ​**a** ‌→ **w** ​— ​Special character
​- ‌**n** ​→ **a** ​— ​Special character
‌- ​**a** → ​**n** ​— Special ‌character
​- ‌**n** → ​**i** ‌— Special ​character
‌- **i** ‌→ ​**n** — ​Special ​character
​- **m** ‌→ ‌**—** — ​Dropped

sources.citation: Iryeon, Samguk Yusa (Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms), 1281; English trans. Ha Tae-Hung and Grafton K. Mintz (1972).

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of ‌the name ‌is **/hwa.nin/** ​— Korean ​Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme ​by phoneme:

​- **hwa** ​— The ‌first syllable ​of Hwanin, ​carrying primary ‌stress in ​the romanised ‌form.
- ​**nin** — ‌The middle ​syllable or ​element, pronounced with ​level pitch ​in Korean.
​- **-** ‌— The ​final syllable, ‌often closing ​in a ‌nasal or ​simple vowel ‌in the ​Korean reading.

‌For the ​modern speaker, ​the closest ‌approximation is: ‌'HWAH-neen' — ‌In Korean reading, ​the first ​syllable is ‌pronounced with ​rounded lips ​and the ‌second is ​short and ​level. The ‌scholarly form  ​Hwanin  preserves ‌the capital ​that marks ​a proper ​name; the ​ASCII form  ‌hananim  is ‌an older ​romanisation still used ‌in domain ​names.

Kindred ​and historical ‌forms of ‌the name:

‌- **Hangul** ‌— 환인 ​— the ‌Korean script ​form.
- ​**Hanja** — ​桓因 — ‌the Sino-Korean ​character form.

​In Korean ​reading, the ‌first syllable is ​pronounced with ​rounded lips ​and the ‌second is ​short and ‌level. The ​scholarly form  ‌Hwanin  preserves ​the capital ‌that marks ‌a proper ​name; the ​ASCII form  ​hananim  is ​an older ‌romanisation still ‌used in ​domain names.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌preserved ‌in Hangul ​as **하나님** ​— ​Korean alphabet, ​attested ​Modern Korean ‌(Hangul ​promulgated 1446 ​CE), ‌in Korea. ​The script ‌is ​written left-to-right.[^1]

‌The ​scholarly transliteration ​is ​*Hananim* (Revised ​Romanization), ​giving the ‌normalized reading ​/ha.na.nim/.

‌The rendering ​proceeds ‌step by ​step:

‌- Standard ​modern ‌Hangul orthography ​for the ​shamanic ‌sky god
‌- ‌Also written ​하느님 ​(Haneullim); 하나님 ‌is ​shared with ​the modern ‌Christian ​usage

Korean ​names ‌may be ​written ‌in Hangul, ​the ​indigenous Korean ​alphabet, and ​sometimes ‌in Hanja, ‌the ​Sino-Korean character ‌set. ​For **Hwanin**, ​the ‌Hangul form ‌is **환인** ‌and ‌the Hanja ​form ‌is **桓因**. ​Hangul ​‘환인’ and ​Hanja ‌‘桓因’, the ​forms used ​in ​the Samguk ‌Yusa; ​the name ​is ​also rendered ‌‘Hananim’ ​(하나님) in ‌Korean vernacular ​usage. ‌The ASCII ​form ‌*hananim* is ‌a ​technological compromise; ​the ​capitalised restoration ​**Hwanin** is ‌the ‌scholarly citation ​form.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Hwanin** ​is the ‌supreme celestial ‌figure who ​rules from ​heaven in ​the Dangun ​founding myth ​in Korean ‌tradition. The ​name means ​"Lord of ‌Heaven" and ​belongs ‌to the ​domain "Supreme ‌God, Heaven." ​In the ​Samguk Yusa, ​Hwanin is ​the ruler ​of heaven ‌who answers ​the Buddha's ‌request for ​a ‌land fit ​for his ‌teachings by ​sending his ‌son Hwanung ​to earth. ​Hwanin is ‌not a ‌creator in ‌the biblical ​sense; he ​is the ‌apex ​of a ​celestial hierarchy ‌that authorises ​the descent ​of culture ‌and law ​to the ‌Korean peninsula.[^1]

​### Lord ​of Heaven

​Hwanin sits ​at ‌the apex ‌of the ​Korean celestial ‌order, the ​source from ​which legitimate ‌authority descends.

‌### Celestial ‌Court

Heaven ‌is imagined ​as a ‌court with ​ministers, ​retainers, and ​an ethical ‌law that ​mirrors human ​government.

### ​Ancestor of ‌Hwanung

Hwanin ​authorises the ​descent that ​makes possible ‌the birth ​of ‌Dangun and ​the founding ‌of Korea.

​### Moral ‌Order

The ‌myth encodes ​the belief ​that rulers ​and peoples ​are accountable ‌to a ‌higher heavenly ​standard.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The mythology ​of Hwanin ‌is preserved ‌in Korean ​oral tradition, ​shamanic ritual ​texts, and ​classical sources ​such as ‌the Samguk ​Yusa. The ​narratives are ‌not merely ​stories; they ‌encode social ​values, ritual obligations, ‌and relationships ​between humans, ​nature, and ​the sacred. ​Some details ​vary by ‌region and ​by shamanic ‌lineage.[^1]

### ​The Request ‌from Heaven ​(Samguk Yusa)

‌According to ​Iryeon's Samguk Yusa, ‌the Buddha ​asked Hwanin ​whether there ‌was a ‌land on ‌earth where ​his teachings ​could flourish. ‌Hwanin looked ​down and ​saw the ‌Korean peninsula, ​then offered ​his son ‌Hwanung to descend ​with heavenly ‌attendants and ​sacred regalia.[^2]

​### The ​Descent of ​Hwanung (Foundation ‌myth)

Hwanin ‌granted Hwanung ​three heavenly ‌seals and ​three thousand ​retainers. Hwanung ‌descended beneath ‌a sandalwood ‌tree on a ‌high mountain, ​bringing laws, ‌grains, and ​the arts ​of civilisation ​to the ‌human world.

​### Hananim ​and Korean ​Religion (Living ‌usage)

The ​vernacular title ​Hananim became ​the standard Korean ‌Christian name ​for God, ‌while in ​folk and ‌shamanic contexts ​Hwanin remains ‌the celestial ‌ancestor of ​the Korean ​people. The ​two usages ​live in ‌parallel, one ‌theological and ​one mythological.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Hwanin ​entered ‌Korean ‌Christian ​vocabulary ​as Hananim, ​the ​name ​for ‌the ​biblical ​God, ‌while ​in ‌shamanic ​and nationalist ‌discourse ​he ​remains ​the ​mythic ​ancestor ‌of ​the ‌Korean people. ​The ‌two ​traditions ‌interpret ​the ‌name ​differently—one ​as ‌a ‌personal deity, ‌the ​other ​as ‌a ​celestial ​title—but ‌both ​preserve ​the ‌sense that ​Korea's ‌legitimacy ​flows ​from ​heaven. ​Confucian ‌and ‌Buddhist ​interpreters ‌have also ​read ​Hwanin ‌through ‌their ‌own ‌categories, ​sometimes ‌as ​a ​personification of ​cosmic ‌principle ​and ​sometimes ​as ‌a ​devotional ​figure.[^1]

​Within the ‌Korean ​tradition, ‌closely ​related ‌names ​in ‌the ‌corpus ​include ​[[baekdusan|Baekdusan]], [[chilsong|Chilsong]], ​[[dangun|Dangun]], ​[[halmoni|Halmoni]], ‌[[hwanung|Hwanung]], ‌and ​[[jowangshin|Jowangshin]].

sources.citation: Iryeon, Samguk Yusa (Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms), 1281; English trans. Ha Tae-Hung and Grafton K. Mintz (1972).

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus is ‌yet ​assigned ​to ‌Hwanin ​with ‌certainty. That ​absence ‌should ​be ​read ​honestly: for ​a ​Korean ‌name ​of ‌this ​type the ‌material ​record ‌is ​expected ‌to be ​thin, ​and ‌the ‌primary ‌evidence ​remains the ​textual ‌testimony ​gathered ​in ‌the Scholarly ​Sources ​section[^1].

‌Were ​such ‌evidence ​to surface, ​it ​would ​take ‌recognizable ‌forms: votive ​or ‌dedicatory ​inscriptions ​naming ‌하나님, ‌sanctuary or ‌cult ‌remains ​tied ‌to ​supreme god ​and ​iconography ‌matching ​its ​traditional ​attributes (the ‌heavens ​and ​the ​sandalwood ‌tree). Each ​candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed ​against ‌the reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.
